Eddie Possehl is a dynamic and driven writer/director with a passion for the written word and all things film, television, comics, and games. His passion for storytelling led him to establish his own production company in hopes of achieving his dreams.
His dedication to his craft has attracted renowned talent like Yuri Lowenthal to collaborate with him on his projects. As he grows and improves, Eddie is a shining example of a self-starter.

Science fiction is one of the greatest, most popular fiction genres of all time. The ability to tell stories that audiences can relate to while taking place in worlds unlike anything they know is a great skill. There are some truly phenomenal sci-fi books across the ages, and it is extremely difficult to compare them all, given how many amazing novels are out there.

It's hard not to love a good sci-fi book, whether one is an avid sci-fi reader or a casual one. If readers are looking for a read that feels perfect from cover-to-cover, then there are more than enough books that they can pick up to enjoy at any time. This is not to compare or make these great pieces of literature compete, but merely a way to show love to stories that really deserve it.

1
'Foundation' (1951)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/foundation-asimov0.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: The cover of the book Foundation

blocks.x: Image via Grafton Books

There's no beating the classics, and one of the greatest is Isaac Asimov's Foundation. It follows a group of human scientists as they try to sustain and defend humanity amidst the fall of the Galactic Empire. With the fear of humanity falling into a new dark age nipping at their heels, Foundation has tension that radiates off of every page.

The themes present in Foundation are excellent, and Asimov does a stellar job executing them. As the characters present in the story use what is called "psychohistory" to predict the future of the human race via math, history, sociology, and more, some real thought-provoking plot points and character arcs come about.

2
'Neuromancer' (1984)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F64c40d5debd38-Screenshot%202022-10-19%20141001.png?fit=crop&w=90&h=90
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/neuromancer-1984-book-cover.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
Image via Orion Publishing Group

Cyberpunk worlds are some of the most popular in sci-fi stories. Worlds that look and feel like the technological future — seen in projects like Blade Runner, Cyberpunk 2077, and more — are some of the most memorable. Neuromancer, a 1984 novel by William Gibson, is argued to be the first novel to be released that can be considered what everyone now knows as cyberpunk. This project truly popularized the modern-day definition of cyberpunk and cyberspace, making it a generational novel.

There's a plethora of style and identity within Neuromancer, and that leads to an unforgettable ride. The characters within it are also two great examples of how to execute anti-hero characters. In fact, this novel is so well-written that Gibson actually achieved what's known as "science fiction's triple crown" for it, winning the Hugo Award, the Philip K. Dick Award, and the Nebula Award.

3
'Frankenstein' (1818)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/frankenstein-book.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: The cover of 'Frankenstein' by Mary Shelley

blocks.x: Image via Castlesync

Mary Shelley's Frankenstein is commonly considered one of the very first sci-fi novels ever written. Brought to life all the way back in 1818, Shelley is also a great example of an excellent early female author. Frankenstein has gone on to be one of the most impactful stories ever written, being adapted countless times in the last 200-something years. Even more times, there have been stories that take heavy inspiration from the plot of this smash hit.

Frankenstein asks countless thought-provoking questions about the human condition, morality and ethics in the pursuit of science, and the cost loneliness can have on living beings. The philosophical ideas thrown in the way of the reader make this a truly engaging read and one that leads them to think about their own lives. Frankenstein is very memorable all across the board and is a genuine masterclass in storytelling.

4
'The Three-Body Problem' (2006)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/the-three-body-problem-liu-cixin-chongqing-publishing-house.png?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Book cover of Liu Cixin's The Three-Body Problem, depicting a futuristic pyramid beneath multiple suns and a star-filled sky.

blocks.x: Image via Tor Books

In 2006, author Liu Cixin wrote The Three-Body Problem, and the world clamored over it — so much so that it has now become a Netflix television hit. This story is incredibly smart, using actual astrophysics — the "three-body problem" being a concept in real-world math and physics — to move its story and concepts forward.

The Three-Body Problem also deals with fun space ideas, such as the "dark forest" theory. There are so many fun sci-fi and space concepts that make this 2006 story feel unique and inventive. This, combined with the use of real-world science, makes this product feel highly engaging throughout the entire read.

5
'Kindred' (1979)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/kindred-octavia-e-butler.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
Image via Beacon Press/Octavia E. Butler

Some of the best sci-fi stories take real-world history and use it to enhance the more supernatural aspects of the world the story takes place in. Kindred, by Octavia E. Butler, takes a sci-fi concept like time travel to make a genuine problem like slavery something impossible for the reader to ignore.

Kindred takes a Black woman named Dana from 1970 all the way back to a Maryland plantation in the 1800s via a time slip. Butler forces the reader to look at the horrors of the topic at hand with unblinking eyes, leading to Kindred being hard to read at times in a way that makes the project unforgettable and beyond compelling.

6
'Cello's Gate' (2025)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/cellos-gate-book-cover.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: The book cover for Cello's Gate by Maurice Africh

blocks.x: Image via Second World Books

Maurice Africh's 2025 novel about the ever-lovable Captain Grey and his crew of space pirates, Cello's Gate is a fun read. Every good sci-fi story needs some good worldbuilding at the center of it, and Cello's Gate is like opening a loot box at every new corner, with so much to enjoy and marvel at.

Cello's Gate is a rip-roaring ride from the first to the final page. The characters are enjoyable, the galaxy is vast, and the action is exciting. For people looking to be among the first to hop onto a new series that will most definitely become the next big thing, there's no question that Africh's Cello's Gate is one of the best spots to look.

7
'The Martian Chronicles' (1950)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/martian-chronicles-book-cover.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: The book cover for The Martian Chronicles by Ray Bradbury

blocks.x: Image via HarperCollins Publishers

Everyone loves a good anthology project, and one of the best sci-fi anthology novels is The Martian Chronicles by Ray Bradbury. It's more accurate to call this a "fix-up novel," though, as the singular stories that make up the anthology are pre-published short stories put together with connective tissue between them to help them come together.

This product from Bradbury is one that tells the story of humanity's numerous attempts to colonize Mars and the resulting negative effect and steady decline of the native Martian civilization. These separate stories come together to tell one large tale about the effect that humanity has on others with their need to colonize and expand.

8
'Stranger in a Strange Land' (1961)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/stranger-in-a-strange-land-book-cover.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: The book cover for Stranger in a Strange Land by Robert A. Heinlein

blocks.x: Image via G. P. Putnam's Sons

Written by Robert A. Heinlein, Stranger in a Strange Land is the story of Valentine Michael Smith, a human born on the planet Mars and raised by the native Martians. Being a true fish-out-of-water story, the protagonist comes to Earth as a young adult, and due to his upbringing, he struggles to understand the planet's customs and how humanity works in general.

What makes Stranger in a Strange Land so special is the fact that it helped push the 1960s and 1970s movements for sexual freedom and anti-establishment. This is also the very first sci-fi novel to make it onto The New York Times bestseller list. If these things aren't a testament to how great this book is, I don't know what is.

9
'Red Rising' (2014)
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/cover-of-red-rising-by-pierce-brown.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Cover of 'Red Rising' by Pierce Brown

blocks.x: Image via Del Rey Books

Without a doubt, Red Rising by Pierce Brown is one of the greatest modern sci-fi franchises of all time. The first book of the same name is one that has gone on to be unforgettable for all the best reasons. Red Rising feels like a mix between The Hunger Games, Game of Thrones, and tales of classic Greek mythology.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/assets/images/sr-db-logo-icon-colored-dark.svg?v=1.9

Darrow O'Lykos is a phenomenally written protagonist who is a joy to watch through everything he does. The setup for his character makes him engaging and someone the reader genuinely wants to root for. The worldbuilding within Brown's series that began here is legendary — truly. This world is something people want to explore more of, which is proof of how talented Brown is as an author.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/dune-frank-herbert-book-cover.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Dune by Frank Herbert book cover.

blocks.x: Image via Ace Books

Currently one of the largest sci-fi film franchises of all time, Dune is a story that has gone on to be one of the most popular and impactful in the entire genre, so much so that it even inspired a ton of Star Wars. Frank Herbert is a highly skilled writer, and it's because of this that Dune has impacted so much of sci-fi as a whole.

Dune is a massively detailed universe that is such a joy to explore via the journey of the engrossing Paul Atreides, played by the one and only Timothée Chalamet in the modern film adaptation. This book takes a deep look at politics, ecology, and organized religion. It feels like a space epic while also being extremely thought-provoking.

Leia is not a supporting character in her own story — she is the moral centre of the entire rebellion.

That same fierce, principled, unbreakable core is what defines you.

The Nostromo · Alien

Ellen Ripley

You are not reckless, not grandiose, and not particularly interested in being anyone's hero — you just refuse to stop when it matters.

You see threats clearly, you document the truth even when no one listens, and when the time comes you handle it yourself.

Ripley's heroism is earned, not performed. She doesn't have a speech — she has a flamethrower and a plan.

You share her composure under the worst possible pressure, and her refusal to pretend the monster isn't there.

When it counts, you don't flinch. That's everything.

The Wasteland · Mad Max

Max Rockatansky

You have been through fire that would break most people — and what came out the other side is something the world underestimates at its peril.

You don't ask for help, don't need validation, and don't wait for anyone to tell you the rules no longer apply.

Your loyalty, when it finally arrives, is absolute — but it's earned in silence and tested in action, not in words.

Max is not a nihilist. He is someone who lost everything and found, against his will, that he still has something worth protecting.

That bruised, stubborn, ultimately human core is exactly yours.

4
'The Three-Body Problem' (2006)

Image via Tor Books

In 2006, author Liu Cixin wrote The Three-Body Problem, and the world clamored over it — so much so that it has now become a Netflix television hit. This story is incredibly smart, using actual astrophysics — the "three-body problem" being a concept in real-world math and physics — to move its story and concepts forward.

The Three-Body Problem also deals with fun space ideas, such as the "dark forest" theory. There are so many fun sci-fi and space concepts that make this 2006 story feel unique and inventive. This, combined with the use of real-world science, makes this product feel highly engaging throughout the entire read.

5
'Kindred' (1979)

Image via Beacon Press/Octavia E. Butler

Some of the best sci-fi stories take real-world history and use it to enhance the more supernatural aspects of the world the story takes place in. Kindred, by Octavia E. Butler, takes a sci-fi concept like time travel to make a genuine problem like slavery something impossible for the reader to ignore.

Kindred takes a Black woman named Dana from 1970 all the way back to a Maryland plantation in the 1800s via a time slip. Butler forces the reader to look at the horrors of the topic at hand with unblinking eyes, leading to Kindred being hard to read at times in a way that makes the project unforgettable and beyond compelling.

6
'Cello's Gate' (2025)

Image via Second World Books

Maurice Africh's 2025 novel about the ever-lovable Captain Grey and his crew of space pirates, Cello's Gate is a fun read. Every good sci-fi story needs some good worldbuilding at the center of it, and Cello's Gate is like opening a loot box at every new corner, with so much to enjoy and marvel at.

Cello's Gate is a rip-roaring ride from the first to the final page. The characters are enjoyable, the galaxy is vast, and the action is exciting. For people looking to be among the first to hop onto a new series that will most definitely become the next big thing, there's no question that Africh's Cello's Gate is one of the best spots to look.

7
'The Martian Chronicles' (1950)

Image via HarperCollins Publishers

Everyone loves a good anthology project, and one of the best sci-fi anthology novels is The Martian Chronicles by Ray Bradbury. It's more accurate to call this a "fix-up novel," though, as the singular stories that make up the anthology are pre-published short stories put together with connective tissue between them to help them come together.

This product from Bradbury is one that tells the story of humanity's numerous attempts to colonize Mars and the resulting negative effect and steady decline of the native Martian civilization. These separate stories come together to tell one large tale about the effect that humanity has on others with their need to colonize and expand.

8
'Stranger in a Strange Land' (1961)

Image via G. P. Putnam's Sons

Written by Robert A. Heinlein, Stranger in a Strange Land is the story of Valentine Michael Smith, a human born on the planet Mars and raised by the native Martians. Being a true fish-out-of-water story, the protagonist comes to Earth as a young adult, and due to his upbringing, he struggles to understand the planet's customs and how humanity works in general.

What makes Stranger in a Strange Land so special is the fact that it helped push the 1960s and 1970s movements for sexual freedom and anti-establishment. This is also the very first sci-fi novel to make it onto The New York Times bestseller list. If these things aren't a testament to how great this book is, I don't know what is.

9
'Red Rising' (2014)

Image via Del Rey Books

Without a doubt, Red Rising by Pierce Brown is one of the greatest modern sci-fi franchises of all time. The first book of the same name is one that has gone on to be unforgettable for all the best reasons. Red Rising feels like a mix between The Hunger Games, Game of Thrones, and tales of classic Greek mythology.

Darrow O'Lykos is a phenomenally written protagonist who is a joy to watch through everything he does. The setup for his character makes him engaging and someone the reader genuinely wants to root for. The worldbuilding within Brown's series that began here is legendary — truly. This world is something people want to explore more of, which is proof of how talented Brown is as an author.

10
'Dune' (1965)

Image via Ace Books

Currently one of the largest sci-fi film franchises of all time, Dune is a story that has gone on to be one of the most popular and impactful in the entire genre, so much so that it even inspired a ton of Star Wars. Frank Herbert is a highly skilled writer, and it's because of this that Dune has impacted so much of sci-fi as a whole.

Dune is a massively detailed universe that is such a joy to explore via the journey of the engrossing Paul Atreides, played by the one and only Timothée Chalamet in the modern film adaptation. This book takes a deep look at politics, ecology, and organized religion. It feels like a space epic while also being extremely thought-provoking.
